credit.credit-words: Intervals
A bit of theory
BH
Intervals describe the difference in pitch between two notes. A melodic interval is the difference between two
notes in a melodic line. A harmonic interval describes the difference between two notes within a single chord.
Other than the distinction of context, melodic and harmonic intervals are pretty much the same thing.
To work out an interval, start by counting the number of
note letters
from the first note to the last, inclusive.
Beyond the octave, it is normal to just start again, so from C up to D is thought of as a 2nd, reguardless of the
number of octaves that might separate them. However in some situations we do talk about 9ths, 11ths and 13ths.
While the class of an interval is determined by counting written notes, the precise quality of an interval depends
on the number of semitones it contains.
An Augmented 4th is also called a tritone, because the notes are three whole tones apart.
Degrees of Dissonance
Intervals can be categorised as being more or less
dissonant.
The word "dissonant" is not a perjorative in this
case, rather it means "requiring resolution". The most consonant (least dissonant) intervals are the unison and
the octave. These are also perfect intervals (P1 and P8). The next most consonant interval is the perfect 5th.
The perfect 4th is odd because in classical music it is considered a dissonance, if it occurs from the bass.
After the perfect consonances come the imperfect consonances. Major and minor 3rds and 6ths are considered
consonant, but not as consonant as the perfect 5th and unison.
Lastly are the true dissonances. The major 2nd and minor 7th are called "mild" dissonances, while the minor 2nd
and major 7th are called "harsh" dissonances. The augmented 4th and diminished 5th are also considered harsh
dissonances.
While I said earlier that there is no real difference between harmonic and melodic intervals, there is one subtle
difference in the way they are categorised by dissonance, the melodic intervals of the 2nd and 7th are not
considered dissonant when they separate notes in a melody. The augmented 4th and diminished 5th were
always considered dissonant, even in a melody.
All of the above should be taken with a large pinch of salt nowadays because of the prevelance of all of these
intervals used unprepared and unresolved in modern music, however if you plan to emulate a classical style, or
even if you need fine control over tension and release in a harmony you should be aware of the distinctions.
Inversions of Intervals
If you take the lower note of an interval and transpose it up in octaves until it lies above the other note, you get a
new interval, as follows:
The thing to notice here is that the inversions are reciprocal, for example inverting a minor 2nd gives a major
7th, and inverting a major 7th gives a minor 2nd.
Enharmonic Equivalence
Consider the interval C♯ - E♭. Because it spans three note letters it is definately a 3rd, but it contains the same
number of semitones as a major 2nd. We call this interval a diminished 3rd (one semitone narrower than a minor
3rd,) and we say it is
enharmonically
equivalent
to a major 2nd.
Continuing, if we take an existing major 3rd and widen it: like F - A♯ or G♭ - B we get an augmented 3rd, which
is enharmonically equivalent to a perfect 4th. It's inversion is a diminished 6th, which is enharmonically a perfect
5th.
The same kind of thing can be done with the other intervals, for example C♯ - D♭ is enharmonically a unison,
but because of the way it is spelt, we call it a diminished 2nd.
Narrowing a diminished interval further (while retaining the same note letters) gives a doubly diminished interval,
and widening an augmented interval gives a doubly augmented one.
While you won't run in to these odd intervals very often, they will crop up from time to time and it's useful
to be able to identify them.
Conclusion
Intervals describe the distances between notes. Knowing intervals gives you an easy way to talk and think
about those distances. You might be wondering what is the point of distinguishing between i.e. an augmented
6th and a minor 7th when they both sound the same, but in functional harmony they are described differently
because of the way they
behave
. To continue the example, an augmented 6th in a chord typically resolves
outwards a semitone in both directions, where a minor 7th (dominant 7th) likes to fall by a 2nd. The way you
spell your chords can be an indication of their intended function.
